Before we start

What your business needs in place.

Advice is only worth its price when these are true.

The decision-maker in the room

Advice relayed second-hand arrives without its reasoning and gets overruled by whoever spoke last. If the person who signs cannot attend, the engagement is worth less than it costs.

Honesty about what has already been decided

If a platform has been chosen and the review is for cover, say so — I will decline rather than write it. Where the decision is genuinely open, that is where this is worth the money.

Access to what is being reviewed

Code, architecture docs, the actual bill, or the proposal on the table. A review conducted on descriptions is a conversation, not an audit, and should not be priced as one.

Willingness to hear 'do not build this'

It is the most common recommendation and the most valuable one. If it is unwelcome, the report will be worth exactly nothing to you.

Terms

How the money and the risk are split.

No retainer to start a conversation, and no invoice for work that never got delivered.

Half to start, half on delivery

Balance falls due when the work is done and handed over. Not delivered, not charged.

Fixed price, not an estimate

The number holds unless you change the scope. If I misjudged it, that is mine.

The clock starts at handover

From the day I have everything on the list, not from the day you pay.

One round of revisions included

Then hourly, quoted before anything starts. No surprise invoices.

You own everything at the end

Code, accounts, assets and credentials. Nothing is held hostage.

Scope

What this is not, and who it is not for.

These are quoted separately, so the price above stays a price.

  • Building anything — that is a separate service, quoted separately
  • Vendor licences and subscriptions
  • Recruitment and placement fees
  • Legal or regulatory sign-off
  • Training data or dataset acquisition
  • Acting as your named technical officer for regulatory purposes

Right fit, wrong fit

Saves a call that would end in no.

A good fit

  • You are about to spend real money and want a second opinion
  • You have an AI system and the bill is climbing
  • You need build-versus-buy answered with numbers
  • You have budget and no senior technical person
  • The decision is genuinely still open

Not a fit

  • You want a report supporting a decision already made
  • Nobody senior can attend
  • You want the deck rather than the thinking
  • You need someone to build it — ask for the build instead

After launch

After the report.

A roadmap ages. Providers ship, prices fall, and the build-versus-buy answer that was right in March is wrong by September. The fractional arrangement is for companies that would rather have that tracked than rediscovered.

Questions

The ones people actually ask.

Do you take commission from vendors?

No, from anyone, ever. It is the whole basis on which this advice is worth paying for, and the moment it were not true the advice would be worthless.

What if you recommend we do nothing?

Then that is the finding, and it is usually the most valuable one. Most AI spending in this market goes on things that a database query or a better process would have solved for a fraction of the price.

How is this different from a big consultancy?

I run the systems I advise on and I write the code. That means the recommendation comes with an implementation cost I would have to honour myself, which is a strong discipline against recommending things that sound good.

Can you also build what you recommend?

Yes, and it is quoted separately and later, so the advice is never a sales route. If you would rather someone else builds it, the roadmap is written to be handed over.

How quickly can you start?

A review is usually days rather than weeks — the value is in answering before the money is committed, and an answer that arrives after the contract is signed is just an expensive opinion.
